lines: {target}? Dry cliffs make every mistake echo.

Red sand and terracotta do not soften a fall.
That tale makes Badlands feel much closer than it did a moment ago.
I will remember Badlands as hard country with old color in its bones.
I would take the terracotta shelves of Badlands in a tight group, with no one hurrying ahead.

If the animals balked at the terracotta shelves of Badlands, I would trust them before my pride.
If word came of a husk wandering in from the dry flats, I would bring the stragglers into the middle.
{target}? You found red cliffs and dry gullies stretching for miles. I can see why that stayed with you.

The dark is bad enough with dry wind humming through narrow ravines beyond the firelight.
Did your provisions last through the journey around red cliffs and dry gullies stretching for miles?

The tale nearly ended around loose sand, sudden drops, and heat with little shade. I am glad you are here.

{target}? Heat makes thirst louder than judgment.

I will remember Desert as dry land that asks too much of the mouth.
I hope the next person listens when you warn them about husks, thirst, and dunes that hide the horizon.
If the group lost the well and its line of torches, we would stop instead of guessing.
A tight flock near the shifting dunes of Desert would warn me before any shout.

I would keep the tale of loose sand hiding sudden drops ready for the next traveler.
I would ask who had eaten before asking what they found at Desert.
No bundle of wool is worth facing a husk crossing the dunes after sunset with the group scattered.
Was there still bread left after the road around open desert where heat and distance blur together?
My pack for Desert would hold bread, wool, and room for wet gear.
Seeing you at the gate would finally quiet my worry about husks, thirst, and dunes that hide the horizon.
I would take the shifting dunes of Desert in a tight group, with no one hurrying ahead.

I understand {target} differently now that you have described open desert where heat and distance blur together.

Before traveling near open desert where heat and distance blur together, I would want water, shade, and travel planned around the sun.
{target}? Wind has carved the land into bad footing.

The thought of the narrow towers of Eroded Badlands will stay with me longer than the treasure in that tale.
I will remember Eroded Badlands as badlands worn sharp by weather.
I would take the narrow towers of Eroded Badlands in a tight group, with no one hurrying ahead.
The walk from thin terracotta spires carved by constant wind back to the sheepfold crosses more than distance.
After a trip near thin terracotta spires carved by constant wind, rounding up a loose lamb sounds peaceful.
The moment we saw a skeleton watching from a high shelf, I would call every name and start moving.
I would divide food by need if crumbly terracotta over deep gullies delayed us.
You found gold and colored terracotta from safer ground and got past crumbly ledges, long drops, and no shade. That is a lot for one trip.
We would not leave the widest canyon leading out until the next safe point was clear.
My pack for Eroded Badlands would hold bread, wool, and room for wet gear.
I would watch the sheep closely before committing anyone to the narrow towers of Eroded Badlands.
I would check packs, people, and the remaining daylight from the base of a broad terracotta spire.
You described wind moaning between tall red columns so clearly that I nearly felt I was there.
No treasure could make me ignore crumbly ledges, long drops, and no shade.
The thought of crumbly terracotta over deep gullies would have me checking the ground every few steps.
After leaving behind thin terracotta spires carved by constant wind, even our muddy sheepfold must have looked welcoming.
Would you have found home without the broad floor of a gully instead of the exposed tops?
{target}? Dry grass takes warning from the wind.

Acacia trees lean like they heard bad news.
A place like Savanna can turn one small mistake into a long walk home.
I will remember Savanna as warm grassland where the wind talks first.
The moment I noticed fire, sudden ravines, and little shade at noon, I would start looking for the way out.
The group should move at the pace of the person most troubled by fire racing through tall dry grass.
I will not call our village dull after hearing about dry grassland dotted with acacia trees.
I would make sure the night watch knew exactly what a pillager watching from the open grass looked like.

I would put a calm traveler beside anyone frightened by fire racing through tall dry grass.
The thought of fire racing through tall dry grass would have me checking the ground every few steps.

Before exploring Savanna, I would make sure everyone could point to a stone wall beneath an acacia.

If every creature grew still near the dry grasslands of Savanna, so would I.
At the acacia line near the village, we could count heads before worry sent us in every direction.
We would agree on a turning time before exploring Savanna.
{target}? High dry ground lets trouble see far.

I will remember Savanna Plateau as dry high land with a long view of danger.
I understand wanting acacia wood and wide views of the country below, though I might have stopped sooner.

One glimpse of a pillager with a clear view uphill would be enough. We would leave together.
Every stop near Savanna Plateau should end with names called and answers heard.

The thought of stone overhangs and sudden drops would have me checking the ground every few steps.

Rushing before checking a low path sheltered behind the hills sounds like a fine way to get lost.
If the flock crowded together near the broken cliffs of Windswept Savanna, I would stop immediately.

One person watches the route and another listens for a pillager watching the narrow climb.
{target}? Trees on badlands still grow in hard country.
If anyone heads for Wooded Badlands, tell them. Watch the drops between trunks.
Wood and red stone make strange neighbors.
The warning about steep red slopes beneath oak trees gives me a very different picture of Wooded Badlands.
I will remember Wooded Badlands as badlands with enough trees to hide the edge.
At the first warning of dust and smoke caught under the trees, I would lead everyone toward a flat shelf under a thick oak.
I would pair everyone up so steep red slopes beneath oak trees could not leave one person unnoticed.
I would keep the tale of steep red slopes beneath oak trees ready for the next traveler.
What first warned you about hidden drops, loose dirt, and dry brush catching fire?
Our first stop near Wooded Badlands should be a flat shelf under a thick oak, not the nearest prize.
You remembered hidden drops, loose dirt, and dry brush catching fire as clearly as wood, gold, and terracotta from the same rough country. Good. People need to hear both parts.
A shepherd learns not to drag nervous animals toward steep red slopes beneath oak trees.
I hope you stopped to eat before you had to deal with hidden drops, loose dirt, and dry brush catching fire.
If we became separated, everyone would return to the oak-lined ridge leading out.
No one keeps good footing for long if the leader rushes through the wooded terracotta ridges of Wooded Badlands.
Our sharpest listener should watch for a skeleton hidden among the trunks.
So that is what {target} is like. I was not expecting oak trees standing above red terracotta canyons.
You sound calm now, but dealing with hidden drops, loose dirt, and dry brush catching fire cannot have felt calm at the time.
Before traveling near oak trees standing above red terracotta canyons, I would want water, an axe, and blocks for the gullies.
